newsitem.title: UK: LPG prices slip, Asia weak as inventories fill up.
newsitem.headline: LPG prices slip, Asia weak as inventories fill up.

text.p: Prices for Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) started to fall in Asia this week, both in the Middle East Gulf and at destinations such as Japan and South Korea, as storage is filling up ahead of the winter, traders said.

The last deal done in East Asia was reported at Saudi Contract Price (CP) +$24 or $25 a tonne C+F Japan for a mixed cargo of 40,000 tonnes, consisting of 50 percent propane and 50 percent butane. The CP is the benchmark price against which most LPG is traded in Asian markets.
But a trader said that there were special factors in this case which reduced the price, and it was representative of a market level of CP +$26 a tonne normally.
Since then, a trader said, levels have fallen steeply. Towards the end of the week, buyers were heard bidding CP +$15 a tonne, against offers at around CP +$23 a tonne C+F Japan.

The reason for the fall is that inventory levels are gradually filling up as players are filling storage from contractual cargoes ahead of the peak winter demand period. As a result the demand for spot supplies is not as great as some had expected, and bids are sliding.

The new CP for July is expected to be announced on Monday. Many expect it to be the lowest level of the year, and in theory this should lead to good buying demand. But with a trader saying that the market has "lost direction" this week, the impact of the new CP at a time of apparently falling spot demand is uncertain.

The weakness is also seen on a fob basis in the Middle East Gulf. The last deal reported done for a small butane piece was at CP -$5.50 a tonne fob Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia. Sellers for both propane and butane are heard at around CP -$3/$4 a tonne fob Gulf, with buyers at around CP -$10. But the market has now become quiet ahead of the publication of the new CP.

The North Sea saw a spate of activity on Thursday before settling down again on Friday. One trader said that a total of 70,000 tonnes of propane was traded on the one day, at between $176 and $177 a tonne cif Northwest Europe on an outright basis.
Of this, around half was said to have gone to a single petrochemical buyer, and the rest was said to be delivered to cavern storage in Sweden for winter coverage.
The price was seen as representative of the market, with sellers still holding out for around $180 a tonne but few buyers or sellers seen.

The storage material was likely to reappear on the market next winter, a trader said. He added that the buyer was likely to be taking it now when prices are relatively cheap in the summer to keep it through the autumn as price levels start building up again and sell it out again when prices peak later in the year.
The only real end-user demand now seen comes from petrochemical buyers, he added, or from traders with short positions into petrochemical buyers who are looking to cover those shorts.
While propane was busy, no butane trade was seen and it was notionally assessed in the low $170's a tonne cif Northwest Europe with a trader describing it as bearish.

As in Asia, the North Sea market was relatively quiet ahead of the new round of posted prices on Friday. No arbitrage is currently seen open to the North Sea from the Mediterranean, and Algerian trade has also been slowed as players await the imminent announcement of state company Sonatrach's prices for July.
